blogs.title: Why AI Might Stop Using Tokens: Inside the Byte Latent Transformer
blogs.description: This post introduces BLT in plain English and explains its big idea: replacing fixed tokenization with raw bytes grouped into dynamic patches. It would cover why tokenization has been a hidden limitation in language models, what changes when models read bytes directly, and how BLT manages to match token-based systems like Llama while avoiding a fixed vocabulary.

blogs.title: Patches, Not Tokens: How BLT Learns to Spend Compute Where It Matters
blogs.description: This post focuses on BLT’s core technical innovation: dynamic patching based on next-byte entropy. It would explain how the model creates longer patches for predictable text and shorter ones for harder parts, using simple examples to show why this is a smarter use of compute than giving every token the same amount of processing.

blogs.title: Can Byte-Level AI Be Faster Too? The Efficiency Story Behind BLT
blogs.description: This post would unpack the paper’s efficiency claims, including how BLT can reduce inference FLOPs by up to 50% while staying competitive in quality. It would explain the architecture’s split between small local byte models and a larger global patch model, and show why larger patches can make inference cheaper without sacrificing too much performance.

blogs.title: Why Byte-Level Models Are Better at Messy Text, Misspellings, and Rare Languages
blogs.description: This post would highlight BLT’s robustness advantages over token-based LLMs. It would cover the paper’s results on noisy text, spelling and character manipulation tasks, phonology, and low-resource translation, showing why direct access to raw bytes helps the model handle edge cases, long-tail inputs, and multilingual variation more naturally.

blogs.title: A New Scaling Law for LLMs? How BLT Changes the Tradeoff Between Model Size and Inference Cost
blogs.description: This post would explore the paper’s broader implication for AI scaling: with BLT, you can grow both patch size and model size while keeping inference cost fixed. It would explain why the authors say patches scale better than tokens, what their scaling experiments showed at up to 8B parameters and 4T training bytes, and why this could matter for the next generation of efficient LLMs.
